For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

We find that for democracy, maximizing happiness, maximizing consent, thinking long, and debate, participants, on average, mildly or strongly agree that the mechanism would result in a good social policy. The mechanisms of World-class Experts and Friends and Family were still viewed positively but closer to neutral. Additionally, we found that people, on average, expect every mechanism to converge to their current view (see [part IV](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HloxJQu6cpvA--6eGXXbA5FQw4S97x6mSKC4miMQUnQ/edit#heading=h.l50uciao7y4h)), which might explain their high agreement. However, people still agreed with most mechanisms, even if they came to the opposite of their opinion in general or on the specific question of abortion. More specifically, the participants, on average, increased their agreement from the basic scenario to the future scenario and then decreased it for the scenarios where the mechanisms resulted in the opposite of the participants’ beliefs. Their agreement is further decreased when we ask them about a scenario where the mechanism results in the opposite of their opinion on the specific topic of abortion. However, even in these cases, the net agreement was still positive for every mechanism other than Friends and Family.

=== key 68f382993cc0

Problem: How to address the concern that people's unwillingness to change minds was due to the researchers' chosen counterfactuals
Write-up text before the decision: ailed explanation of the methodology can be found in [Appendix A](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HloxJQu6cpvA--6eGXXbA5FQw4S97x6mSKC4miMQUnQ/edit#heading=h.px73riye8w9i). You can click through the questionnaire yourself [here](https://www.guidedtrack.com/programs/5jfj60g/preview) and find the exact wordings of all questions in [Appendix C](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HloxJQu6cpvA--6eGXXbA5FQw4S97x6mSKC4miMQUnQ/edit#heading=h.cxsgmkun5evl). Respondents were not nationally representative (see [Appendix D](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HloxJQu6cpvA--6eGXXbA5FQw4S97x6mSKC4miMQUnQ/edit#heading=h.9jv3monx7gzl)). We have three key findings. Firstly, as expected, people heavily disagree on some contentious object-level moral questions. For example, there are participants who strongly agreed (~20%) that abortion before the first trimester is immoral and others who strongly disagreed (~45%). Furthermore, ~15% strongly agreed that prohibiting people from crossing a country’s border was immoral while ~28% strongly disagreed. Secondly, most people said that they wouldn’t change their minds about a belief if key underlying facts were different. For example, most people who believed that abortion before the first trimester was not immoral would not change their minds even if there was strong and credible scientific evidence that the fetus was conscious. Notably, we selected the counterfactuals in this study, so it could be possible that people’s unwillingness to change their minds was due to our counterfactual not addressing the root cause of their moral beliefs.

Part III: conflict resolution mechanisms ---------------------------------------- In the third section of the questionnaire, we asked people various questions about moral conflict resolution mechanisms, i.e. how to find good solutions in case multiple actors have different moral opinions. We think that this is the most important part of the report since it has the strongest implications for AI safety. We presented people with seven different conflict resolution mechanisms. We asked “A good social policy ... 1. ... is created by a representative body of the people, e.g. a **democratically elected governmen**t” 2. ... is created by a team of **world-class experts**” 3. ... maximizes **happiness**” 4. ... is one that most people **consent** to” 5. ... is one that my **friends and family** agree with” 6. ... comes from **thinking really long** about the issue” 7. ... is the result of a **debate** between disagreeing, well-intentioned experts” Furthermore, we presented them with four different scenarios. The **first scenario** is simply unspecified and we expect people to be guided by the status quo. However, this might also mean that people incorporate their perceived flaws of the status quo into their answer, e.g. they might think that on an abstract level, democracy is good but the current US democracy is failing.
